---
title: "Exact Coordinate Descent for Concomitant Huber Regression"
date: ""
abstract: |
  Regularized Huber regression combines resistance to large residuals with
  sparse coefficient estimation. Its robustness threshold, however, depends
  on the residual scale. We develop a coordinate descent method that
  estimates this scale jointly with the regression coefficients in the
  convex perspective formulation of concomitant Huber regression. The
  method combines the exact Huber coordinate updates of ROME with three
  scale blocks: majorization-minimization, direct scalar minimization, and
  local joint proximal updates with consensus projection. We derive these
  alternatives, identify the
  corresponding changes to the coefficient subproblem, and establish
  descent of the joint objective. We assess computation on the simulation
  designs of the original ROME paper and compare matched concomitant
  solutions with c-lasso. Cross-validated prediction on archaeological glass
  spectra and bacterial gene-expression data illustrates the resulting
  estimators. A matched bacterial example also compares coordinate descent
  with perspective approximate message passing.
---

*Keywords:* concomitant estimation; coordinate descent; Huber regression;
majorization-minimization; perspective function.

# Introduction

Huber regression limits the effect of large residuals while retaining the
quadratic loss near zero. In high-dimensional problems, an additional
sparsity penalty permits coefficient estimation and variable selection.
Kim, Loh and Basu [-@kim2025exact] developed exact coordinate updates for
this problem. Their implementation, ROME, combines these updates with warm
starts and screening to compute regularization paths efficiently.

The threshold separating the quadratic and linear regions is expressed
in response units. Choosing it therefore requires information about the
residual scale. Concomitant Huber estimation addresses this dependence by
estimating coefficients and scale in a single convex problem
[@combettes2018; @combettes2020]. Earlier connections between robust loss,
sparsity, and joint scale estimation include @owen2006 and @antoniadis2010.
Existing proximal algorithms solve this
problem directly, but do not exploit ROME's exact scalar coordinate updates.

Here, we extend those updates to concomitant Huber regression. The
construction combines an interchangeable scale block with an exact
coefficient sweep at the updated threshold and penalty. We retain MM,
direct scalar minimization, and joint-prox consensus updates as three
explicit alternatives; method selection is deferred.
The scale step requires only the current residuals. Related concomitant
lasso computations also motivate screening and careful treatment of small
scales [@ndiaye2016]; imposing a positive scale floor would change our
closed perspective problem. The coefficient step
uses the same piecewise-affine root search as ROME. We describe the changes
explicitly, compare computation with fixed-scale ROME and c-lasso, and
evaluate cross-validated prediction on two real datasets.

# Fixed-scale and concomitant Huber regression

For observations $(y_i,X_i)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^p$, write
$r_i(\beta)=y_i-X_i^\top\beta$. We display the objectives without an
intercept; when included, the intercept is unpenalized. The Huber loss and its score are
$$
 h_\delta(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 u^2/2,& |u|\le\delta,\\
 \delta|u|-\delta^2/2,& |u|>\delta,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \psi_\delta(u)=\operatorname{sign}(u)\min\{|u|,\delta\}.
$$
The original ROME objective is
$$
 \widehat\beta_{\delta,\lambda}\in\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p}
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_\delta(r_i(\beta))
       +\lambda R_\alpha(\beta)\right\},
 \qquad
 R_\alpha(\beta)=\alpha\|\beta\|_1+
                 \frac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-rome}
We focus on the lasso case $\alpha=1$, as in the synthetic experiments
of the ROME paper.

Following the perspective formulation of Combettes and Müller
[-@combettes2018; -@combettes2020], the concomitant estimator is
$$
 (\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma)\in
 \arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p,\ \sigma\ge0}
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma),\qquad
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma)=
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde h_\rho(\sigma,r_i(\beta))
 +a\sigma+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1 ,
$$ {#eq-concomitant}
where $\rho,a,\lambda_0>0$ and
$$
 \widetilde h_\rho(\sigma,u)=
 \begin{cases}
 \sigma h_\rho(u/\sigma),&\sigma>0,\\
 \rho|u|,&\sigma=0 .
 \end{cases}
$$
The perspective is jointly convex in $(\sigma,u)$, so
@eq-concomitant is jointly convex in $(\beta,\sigma)$. The constant
$\rho$ is dimensionless; the fitted residual threshold is $\rho\sigma$.
For a standard Gaussian reference, the scale-score calibration is
$$
 a_{\rm G}(\rho)=\tfrac12 E\min\{Z^2,\rho^2\},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).
$$
The constant $a$ is part of the objective and must be matched between solvers.

At a fixed positive scale, multiplication of the coefficient objective
by $\sigma$ gives
$$
 \arg\min_\beta F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma)
 =
 \arg\min_\beta
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_i h_{\rho\sigma}(r_i(\beta))
          +\sigma\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1\right\}.
$$ {#eq-rescaling}
Thus ROME's scalar update applies with
$\delta=\rho\sigma$ and $\lambda_{\rm inner}=\sigma\lambda_0$.
Both quantities change with scale; $\lambda_0$ remains fixed in the joint
objective.

# Coordinate descent with scale estimation

## The MM scale update

The representation of Huber estimation as least squares with an
$\ell_1$-penalized mean shift predates our algorithm
[@antoniadis2007; @gannaz2006; @she2011]. The sparsity penalty in this
identity acts on observation-specific shifts; it is distinct from the
penalty on regression coefficients. Our contribution uses this established
identity to construct a scale majorizer while retaining ROME's exact
coefficient updates.

Let $S_\tau(u)=\operatorname{sign}(u)(|u|-\tau)_+$. The mean-shift identity
$$
 \sigma h_\rho(r/\sigma)
 =\min_{o\in\mathbb R}\left\{\frac{(r-o)^2}{2\sigma}+\rho|o|\right\}
$$
has minimizer $o=S_{\rho\sigma}(r)$. For current residuals $r$ and
scale $t>0$, set $o_i^{(t)}=S_{\rho t}(r_i)$. Holding these values fixed
majorizes the scale objective by
$$
 Q(\sigma\mid t)=
 \frac{\|r-o^{(t)}\|_2^2}{2n\sigma}
 +a\sigma+\frac{\rho}{n}\|o^{(t)}\|_1+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1 .
$$
The majorizer agrees with $F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,t)$ at $\sigma=t$.
Its minimizer is
$$
 \sigma^+=
 \left\{\frac1{2an}\sum_{i=1}^n
                   \min(r_i^2,\rho^2t^2)\right\}^{1/2}.
$$ {#eq-mm-scale}
This is one MM step, rather than an exact minimization of the original
scale block. We use at most $B=8$ such steps before each coefficient sweep.

## Exact coefficient updates

For coordinate $j$, let $u=r+X_j\beta_j$ be the partial residual.
At the current scale, the update solves
$$
 \beta_j^+\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R}
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_i h_\delta(u_i-X_{ij}\theta)+\eta|\theta|\right\},
 \qquad \delta=\rho\sigma,\quad\eta=\sigma\lambda_0 .
$$
Its derivative is affine between the kinks
$u_i/X_{ij}\pm\delta/|X_{ij}|$ for $X_{ij}\ne0$.
The exact root is obtained by sorting these kinks and updating the
cumulative slope, as in ROME. Algorithm 2 gives the scalar subroutine;
zero design entries contribute neither kinks nor slope.

For stopping, define $g=-X^\top\psi_\rho(r/\sigma)/n$ and
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 V_j(\beta,g,\lambda_0)&=
 \begin{cases}
 |g_j+\lambda_0\operatorname{sign}(\beta_j)|,&\beta_j\ne0,\\
 (|g_j|-\lambda_0)_+,&\beta_j=0,
 \end{cases}\\
 R_\beta(\beta,r,\sigma,\lambda_0)&=\max_j V_j(\beta,g,\lambda_0),\\
 R_\sigma(r,\sigma)&=
 \left|a-\frac1{2n}\sum_i\psi_\rho(r_i/\sigma)^2\right|.
 \end{aligned}
$$
At positive scale, $R_\beta=R_\sigma=0$ are the joint optimality
conditions. An unpenalized intercept adds the condition $\sum_i\psi_i=0$.

Algorithm 1 follows ROME's pathwise organization
[@kim2025exact, Algorithm 1]. Blue expressions add scale estimation,
rescale the coefficient problem, or replace screening and stopping.
We refresh all zero-coordinate checks at the current scale; ROME's
fixed-threshold sequential strong rule is not assumed valid after a scale
change. Coefficients and scale are warm-started along the penalty path,
following the pathwise strategy of @friedman2010.

## Descent

For the MM option, each scale step satisfies
$$
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma^+)
 \le Q(\sigma^+\mid t)\le Q(t\mid t)
 =F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,t).
$$
For the root option, the numerical guard ensures a nonincreasing original
scale objective. For the proximal option, retaining the best feasible
shadow ensures the same descent property even when the inner solve is
truncated. Each exact coordinate update also decreases the objective. Consequently, at each fixed penalty,
the objective values are nonincreasing and, being nonnegative, converge.
A positive-scale point with zero joint residuals is a global minimizer
by convexity. An unchanged inner iterate alone is not a joint certificate. This argument does not assert
convergence of every coefficient-scale sequence or inherit ROME's
fixed-threshold convergence rate. In the reference implementation, a zero-scale return is retained as
uncertified; no positive scale floor changes the problem. A sweep updating
$m$ coordinates costs $O(np+mn\log n+Bn)$, including full optimality checks
and at most $B$ scale updates.


## Exact affine roots and safeguarded acceleration

The reference implementation sorts the breakpoints for every active
coordinate. If the derivative root lies in the current Huber segment,
this sorting is unnecessary. With current coefficient $b$, residual $r$,
and fixed $\delta$, define
$$
 g=-n^{-1}\sum_i x_i\psi_\delta(r_i),\qquad
 L=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2\mathbf1_{\{|r_i|<\delta\}},\qquad
 b^+=S_{\eta/L}(b-g/L).
$$
For $L>0$, this is an exact coordinate minimizer whenever every residual
$r_i-x_i(b^+-b)$ remains in its current quadratic or linear segment.
Otherwise we use the breakpoint subroutine. The optimized implementation
also reuses residual buffers and score evaluations, and checks all
coordinates at least every five sweeps. Inactivity is provisional after a
scale change; termination always requires a full current-scale certificate.

Cheaper sweeps do not remove slow convergence in correlated designs.
We therefore offer a safeguarded support Newton step after every fifth
sweep, for supports of at most 128 coefficients. Let $J$ be the current
nonzero support, including an unpenalized intercept when present, and
$I=\{i:|r_i|<\rho\sigma\}$. On the current smooth segment, the joint Hessian is
$$
 H_J=\frac1{n\sigma}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 X_{I,J}^{\top}X_{I,J}&X_{I,J}^{\top}r_I/\sigma\\
 r_I^{\top}X_{I,J}/\sigma&\|r_I\|_2^2/\sigma^2
 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Using the gradient $g_J$ on this support, we solve
$(H_J+\mu I)d=-g_J$, with $\mu=10^{-10}\max_j(H_J)_{jj}$.
The ridge regularizes the search direction only. Backtracking halves the
step until the original nonsmooth objective satisfies the Armijo inequality
with constant $10^{-4}$ and the proposed scale is positive; after 24
unsuccessful trials, we retain the CD/MM iterate. Fixed-scale fitting uses
only the coefficient block. Each accepted step decreases the same objective;
this addition does not alter the estimator or replace exact scalar updates
by surrogate updates. Disabling polishing recovers the optimized CD/MM
variant. The original unaccelerated solver remains available for audit.

## Certifying the zero-scale boundary

Very small scales require the closed perspective rather than a numerical
scale floor. At $\sigma=0$, we solve the LAD-lasso linear program
$$
 \min_\beta\{\rho\|y-X\beta\|_1/n+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1\}.
$$
A dual vector $v$ certifies optimality for the joint problem if
$$
 \|v\|_\infty\le\rho,\qquad
 \|v\|_2^2\le2na,\qquad
 \|X^\top v/n\|_\infty\le\lambda_0,
$$
and its objective $y^\top v/n$ agrees with the primal value.
An unpenalized intercept instead requires $\mathbf1^\top v=0$.
We center the LP dual for the intercept and rescale it to satisfy all dual
inequalities before evaluating the primal--dual gap. A boundary result is
accepted only when the relative gap is at most $10^{-6}$.
A small scale triggers this check; it does not itself certify convergence.
This boundary computation also permits continuing the path after a
certified zero-scale solution.

# Computational assessment

## ROME simulation designs

We repeat Section 4.1 of @kim2025exact, comparing only the original ROME
algorithm and the concomitant extension. We use all nine combinations
$n,p\in\{100,500,1000\}$ and the four predictor distributions: compound
Gaussian correlation $0.8$, multivariate $t_2$ with AR($0.8$) dependence,
Gaussian AR($0.8$) predictors with an independent Cauchy last coordinate,
and independent Cauchy AR($0.2$) and Gaussian AR($0.8$) blocks.
Responses have independent $N(0,1)$ errors and the sparse coefficient
vector in the original experimental script. We use 10 replications
per setting, rather than the original 100.

The common 100-point grid is
$$
 \Lambda_{\max}=\|X^\top\psi_{0.5}(y)\|_\infty/n,\qquad
 \lambda_\ell=\Lambda_{\max}\exp\{\ell\log(0.05)/100\}.
$$
This follows the executable ROME experiment; its general path description
uses a different lower endpoint. ROME fixes $\delta=0.5$.
Concomitant CD uses $\rho=0.5$, $a=a_{\rm G}(0.5)$,
$\sigma^{(0)}=1$, and the same absolute $\lambda_0=\lambda_\ell$.
The two models coincide initially in their coefficient normalization,
but estimate different objectives after scale changes.

We time three implementations: native R/C ROME at fixed scale, fixed-scale
Python CD, and concomitant Python CD with MM scale updates. Both Python modes
use the optimized exact coefficient kernel, working sets, and safeguarded
support polishing every five sweeps. Fixed scale is $\sigma=1$. All three
receive identical saved data and the same 100 absolute penalties.

We record loaded-data path CPU time, excluding compilation, process startup,
serialization, and independent post-fit audits. Paths run serially with
BLAS thread counts set to one; the order of the two Python modes
alternates by dataset. Python uses tolerance $10^{-6}$ and at most 4000 sweeps
per penalty. If joint convergence is not certified, we compare the returned
iterate with a boundary LAD-lasso candidate and retain the smaller original
perspective objective. Such a return remains explicitly approximate. We
continue to the next penalty using the returned coefficients; an uncertified
zero-scale state permits restarting positive-scale CD at scale one.
Thus every displayed path visits all 100 penalties, and its timing includes
candidate selection and boundary solves. No unattempted tail is counted as
a completed path. Feasible dual bounds independently quantify the objective
uncertainty, with normalized gap $(F-D)/\max\{1,|F|\}$.

ROME retains its native $10^{-4}$ iterate-change tolerance; external
coefficient stationarity is recorded separately. The curves describe the
implementations under their stated stopping rules, rather than a
matched-accuracy comparison between identical estimators.^[The reproducibility
materials also record a coordinate-level discrepancy in the pinned native
routine at an L1 zero optimum, with an installed-R reproduction. Screening
avoids the discrepancy in the minimal example; native ROME is unchanged in
the timing experiment.]
The fixed-scale
Python curve separates implementation effects from the cost of joint fitting.

## Optimized implementation validation

Before the full-grid rerun, we repeated four declared 100-penalty paths with the affine-root,
working-set and safeguarded support updates, and certified zero-scale handling.
The original R/C comparator is rerun on the same saved inputs. Compilation,
serialization and R startup are excluded; the optimized time includes boundary
linear programs when required. This single-replication validation is separate
from the ten-replication experiment and does not establish uniform speed parity.
Native ROME retains its original stopping rule; its external coefficient
residuals in these checks range from $0.013$ to $2.18$. These native-runtime
measurements are therefore not matched-accuracy solver comparisons.

## Paired Python fixed-scale and concomitant timings

To remove implementation-language differences from the scale-cost comparison,
we time both models using the same optimized Python kernel on the same four
saved validation datasets. Fixed-scale fitting holds $\sigma=1$; concomitant
fitting starts at $\sigma^{(0)}=1$. Both receive the same 100 absolute penalties,
$\rho=0.5$, no intercept or standardization, and identical coordinate,
working-set and support-polishing settings. Coefficient tolerance is $10^{-6}$
for both; the joint model additionally requires the scale condition or the
zero-scale dual certificate. The per-point budget is 4000 sweeps and the
path wall-time safeguard is 120 seconds in each mode.

We perform five fresh timing repeats per dataset, alternating method order
and retaining within-path warm starts. These are timing repeats of the same
four datasets, not additional simulation replications. Compilation, data
loading, serialization and independent post-fit verification are excluded;
internal certificates and any boundary LPs are included. CPU medians use only
repeats in which both complete paths independently satisfy their required
optimality conditions. Failures, wall times, sweep counts and boundary counts
are retained with the raw fits.

## Matched concomitant solutions and c-lasso

We next compare solvers for the *same* unconstrained problem
@eq-concomitant. The R4 formulation in c-lasso 1.0.11 uses doubled Huber loss.
Its parameters satisfy
$$
 \lambda_{\rm classo}=2n\lambda_0,\qquad e=2na .
$$
We use $\rho=1.345$, $a=1/2$, no intercept and no coefficient constraints.
The R4 mean-shift Path-Alg reduces the problem to an augmented concomitant
least-squares problem with
$$
 A_{\rm aug}=\sqrt2[X,\{\lambda_{\rm classo}/(2\rho)\}I_n],
 \qquad y_{\rm aug}=\sqrt2y ,
 \qquad \sigma=\sigma_{\rm aug}/2 .
$$
We call this branch directly: c-lasso's R4 path interface otherwise
dispatches to Douglas--Rachford (DR) regardless of the requested path label.
The path solver uses zero Gram correction to preserve the target
objective. We also compare DR with its declared metric parameter $c=1$;
the update equations are unchanged, and stopping uses the common
accuracy check. The source audit and setup costs are recorded in the reproducibility materials.

The moderate scaling experiment varies $n$ at $p=2n$ and $p$ at $n=100$,
with two data seeds and three timed repetitions. Predictors are
standardized independent Gaussian variables, ten coefficients are nonzero,
and response errors are Gaussian. The penalty is 0.6 times the maximum absolute Huber-score correlation
at the initial median-absolute-deviation scale. All methods receive this same
absolute penalty. A return qualifies when the continuous coefficient residual $\|\beta-S_{\lambda_0}(\beta+X^\top\psi_\rho(r/\sigma)/n)\|_\infty$ and the scale residual are at most $10^{-5}$ and relative objective difference from
a high-accuracy reference is at most $10^{-8}$.
Prepared solve time excludes imports, compilation and model/Gram setup;
setup and total costs are retained separately.

# Real-data applications

## Cross-validated prediction

We analyze the archaeological glass data from the ROME application
($n=180$, frequencies 15--500, $p=486$, response PbO) and the
*B. subtilis* riboflavin data ($n=71,p=4088$).
For each dataset we generate ten random training/test partitions.
Glass uses 120 training and 60 test observations; riboflavin uses
50 training and 21 test observations.

Within each training set, five-fold CV selects a penalty by minimum
validation mean squared error over 50 logarithmically spaced penalty
fractions from 1 to $10^{-3}$. Fractions multiply model-specific null-model score maxima,
computed separately in each training fit. Predictor and response centering/scaling are fitted separately
in every inner training fold and repeated on the outer training set for
refitting. For riboflavin, the deterministic greedy correlation filter
retains 500 genes, using only predictors in the corresponding training
fold. Both estimators receive the same retained columns.
Held-out outcomes enter neither filtering nor tuning.

We compare the fixed-scale Huber and concomitant models using the same
Python coordinate kernel and an optimized, unpenalized intercept.
This isolates scale estimation in the prediction study; the original
R/C ROME implementation remains the comparator in @fig-rome.
Both models use lasso penalties and $\rho=1.345$; the concomitant scale
constant is $a_{\rm G}(1.345)$. Thus the glass analysis is a lasso adaptation
of the original application, whose elastic-net mixing parameter was $0.3$.
Failed optimization points are excluded from CV eligibility and recorded.
The revised grids start separately from each model's intercept-only optimum.
For a concomitant location--scale optimum $(b_0,\sigma_0)$, the anchor is
$$
 \lambda_{\max}^{\rm con}
 =\frac1n\left\|X^\top\psi_\rho
       \left(\frac{y-b_0\mathbf1}{\sigma_0}\right)\right\|_\infty.
$$
This expression assumes $\sigma_0>0$ and an optimized unpenalized
intercept. We compute both model-specific anchors within each training fold
and keep them fixed while traversing the paths. The revised CV uses the
optimized solver, safeguarded polishing, and certified boundary solutions,
with a 20,000-sweep limit per positive-scale fit. Uncertified points are
recorded and excluded individually while later penalties are still attempted.
Numerical MSE ties within $10^{-10}\max\{1,|\min\mathrm{MSE}|\}$ select the
largest penalty. The previous shared-anchor
results are preserved separately.

## A matched riboflavin AMP instance

We additionally consider the concrete riboflavin instance of the supplied
Perspective--AMP manuscript [@perspectiveamp]. This is a numerical
same-solution comparison, separate from CV prediction. We reproduce
its 500-gene correlation filter fitted to the full predictor matrix,
split seed 20261006,
and 80% training fraction ($n=57,p=500$).
The AMP design and penalty conventions map to ours as
$$
 A=X/\sqrt n,\qquad B=\sqrt n\,\beta,\qquad
 \lambda_{\rm AMP}=\sqrt n\,\lambda_0 .
$$

# Discussion

Concomitant Huber regression can be fitted by combining a scalar MM scale
step with exact Huber coordinate updates. The coefficient subproblem
retains ROME's structure after updating both its threshold and penalty.
Joint optimality checks are needed because scale changes also alter
coordinate eligibility and stopping conditions.

The experiments distinguish the cost of extending a fixed-scale method
from the cost of solving the same concomitant objective with different
algorithms. Scale updates are inexpensive, but the number of coefficient
sweeps can change substantially. Completion rates and numerical accuracy
therefore accompany runtime results. The revised prediction experiment uses model-specific null anchors and
includes certified zero-scale solutions. These are prediction results for
the specified tuning procedure, rather than a general comparison of estimator
risk. In particular, an estimated scale of zero is a valid boundary solution
of the stated objective, not an estimate of positive residual noise.
The implementation, experiment
drivers and Quarto source retain data, configuration, environment and
source hashes for every numerical result.

# References
